title: The labor anthropogony convergence
statement: The Sumerian anthropogonies (the Song of the Hoe; Enki and Ninmah), the Babylonian Atrahasis, and Genesis 2 converge on a specific structure: humans shaped from the earth, on purpose, to carry the gods' toil — with Atrahasis adding the mixed-in god ('that god and man may be mixed together in the clay'); the corpus reads the convergence as transformed memory of a purposive creation, consistent with the canon's account of humanity's making, at the inferred grade the reading can actually carry.

includes: The textual convergence at its own strength: made-from-earth, on-purpose, to-labor, across the four named text-families — most held in project digitization
The Atrahasis distinctive: the slaughtered god's flesh, blood, and intelligence in the clay, read as the tradition's own statement that the made being carries its makers' substance
The memory reading, inferred: the convergence as transformed memory of purposive creation, engaging the labor row already anchored in the woh-claim-0002 apparatus (ATRA-WOH-I:195)
The boundary against 0002: this record reads the anthropogony structure; collective identity across traditions remains 0002's separate burden
excludes: The genetic-engineering vocabulary as a textual claim; the canon's laboratory account is the framework layer other records carry, and this record's texts speak of clay, blood, and toil
Literary-dependence resolution among the four families; the documented Mesopotamian-to-Genesis stream is conceded where documented and not adjudicated where not
Any claim that Genesis shares Atrahasis's labor-relief motive; the 0002 evidence map's finding that Genesis's motive differs is preserved, not overridden
Worldwide extension beyond the named families (Ovid, the Popol Vuh, and Hesiod's Pandora are the article's comparanda, carried as resemblance only)

source_references.locator: ATRA-WOH-I:194-195 (the yoke and the labor of the gods); I:223-225 (the slaughtered god in the clay; 'that god and man may be mixed together in the clay')
GEN-WOH-2:7 (dust from the ground); 2:15 (to work it and keep it)
The Song of the Hoe and the Sumerian anthropogony corpus in the standard anthology
Enki and Ninmah: the clay-shaping and the purpose
The canon's purposive-creation account, against which the convergence is read
Clifford's comparative treatment of the ancient Near Eastern creation accounts, covering the anthropogony family this record reads

alternatives.statement: Clay-shaping is the potter's craft projected onto anthropogony wherever pottery exists; the convergence is a shared topos, not a memory.
The labor motive theologizes Mesopotamian temple economy (humans as the gods' workforce because temples had workforces); Genesis's different motive shows the structure is not stable.
The documented literary stream explains the Near Eastern convergence; the Sumerian-to-Genesis line needs no remembered event.

revision_triggers: Claim woh-claim-0001 or woh-claim-0002 is revised or retired.
Source-language review changes the cited Atrahasis or Genesis observations.
Inspection of the Sumerian texts (currently metadata_only) changes the convergence's shape.
Public prose begins using genetic-engineering vocabulary as textual content, which this record excludes.
